PHSCS 587

Parabolic and Dirac bands

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a linear band crossing differs from a parabolic band edge

An effective-mass parabola is one local band model. Near an ordinary parabolic minimum, E − E0 = ℏ²k²/(2m*) and group velocity grows with k. Near an ideal graphene Dirac point, the low-energy branches are approximately E± − ED = ±ℏvF|k|, where ED is the crossing energy and vF is a characteristic velocity. Wave vector k is measured relative to the relevant extremum or crossing.

Because velocity is (1/ℏ)∇kE, the ideal linear model has a nearly constant speed magnitude vF on each branch, with direction determined by k and branch. A constant parabolic effective mass obtained from a nonzero second derivative is therefore not the suitable starting model at the crossing. Real bands have limits to the linear approximation.

Dimensionality and dispersion together determine DOS. A two-dimensional parabolic band has constant DOS above its edge, whereas an ideal two-dimensional Dirac spectrum has DOS proportional to |E − ED|. A confined nanotube requires its own allowed circumferential wave vectors and subbands; its gap depends on structure. Semimetal band overlap and a zero-gap point crossing are distinct possible band arrangements.

Example

In the ideal 2D Dirac model, moving twice as far in energy from ED doubles the DOS magnitude. The corresponding 2D parabolic-band DOS stays constant within one subband.

Practice

1. Why is the 2D constant-DOS formula for a parabolic band unsuitable at an ideal Dirac point?

Inspect the assumed energy-versus-wave-vector relation.

That formula assumes E − E0 proportional to k². A linear dispersion changes the relationship between k-space state count and energy, producing a DOS proportional to energy distance from the crossing.
